note: Dropped intensifier: 'a most alarming spectacle' became 'an alarming spectacle'.
replacement: The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present a most alarming spectacle. The movement carrying them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so fast that it cannot be guided. Their fate is in their own hands, though in a little while it may no longer be. The first duty of those who direct our affairs at this time is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to replace its inexperience with a knowledge of practical affairs, and its blind impulses with an understanding of its true interests; to adapt its government to time and place; and to change it to suit the events and the people of the age. A new science of politics is needed for a new world. Yet this is what we think about least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we stubbornly fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the abyss.

'the manners of the time' (moeurs) should be customs/habits per style note.
replacement: While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, governed the nations of Europe in peace, society had, amid its misery, several advantages that are now hard to appreciate or even imagine. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince’s tyranny. The monarch felt that the multitude saw him as almost divine, and the respect he inspired gave him a reason to use his power justly. However high they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking the calm and kindly interest in its fate that a shepherd takes in his flock. Without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people had never conceived of a social condition different from their own, and they did not expect ever to rank with their chiefs. They accepted benefits from their superiors without questioning their rights. They grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and they submitted to their exactions without resistance or servility, as to the unavoidable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the habits of the time had also created a kind of law amid the violence and set certain limits to oppression. The noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the unchangeable order of nature. It is therefore easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently endowed by fate. Inequality and misery existed in society then, but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by exercising power or debased by the habit of obeying. They are corrupted by exercising a power they believe to be illegitimate, and by obeying a rule they consider usurped and oppressive. On one side were wealth, strength, and leisure, along with the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other were labor and a crude ignorance. Yet among this coarse and ignorant multitude it was not uncommon to find energetic passions, generous feelings, deep religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic organized in this way could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

note: 'institutions and manners of the nation' (moeurs) should be customs.
replacement: But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks are mingling. The divisions that once separated mankind are being lowered, property is being divided, power is shared, the light of intelligence is spreading, and the abilities of all classes are being cultivated equally. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and customs of the nation. I can imagine a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws, of which they are the common authors. The authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the subject’s loyalty to the chief magistrate would be not a passion but a calm and rational conviction. Every individual would possess rights he is sure to keep, and a kind of manly confidence and mutual courtesy would arise among all classes, equally far from pride and from baseness. The people, well aware of their true interests, would accept that to enjoy the advantages of society they must meet its demands. In such a state of things, the voluntary association of citizens could take the place of the individual efforts of the nobles, and the community would be protected equally from anarchy and from oppression.
